items.title: I’m a priest. Silicon Valley’s search for the ‘soul’ of AI is deeply troubling | Rev Kevin Deal

Last month, religious leaders from across San Francisco gathered behind closed doors to discuss what it means to be human in the age of artificial intelligence.

Anthropic, the AI company operating only a couple of miles from my parish, has been courting priests, rabbis and theologians. Its billionaire cofounder, Christopher Olah, has even pressed Vatican advisers to take seriously the possibility that his company’s chatbot might possess consciousness.

items.title: ‘Shakespearean tale of ego, greed and ambition’: the scandalous story of televangelism
items.summary:
Netflix documentary Primetime Preacher$ travels back to a time when evangelism found a dominant place on US television – and the shocking tabloid stories that followed

For three decades, film-maker Joe Berlinger has gripped true-crime buffs with his deep dives into small-town murders and infamous serial killers. His Netflix explorations of John Wayne Gacy and Jeffrey Dahmer helped flip documentary storytelling from viewer homework to a welcome distraction.

After dedicating so much time to the life of Jeffrey Epstein, the kidnapping of JonBenét Ramsey and other unsolved mysteries, Berlinger thought Primetime Preacher$, his new Netflix documentary on America’s televangelist boom, would offer a break. But it turns out that’s a pretty juicy crime story too, about the religious right’s bank job on American politics. “The deeper resonance for me came when I realized that the global televangelism rise actually mirrors the rise of the religious right,” he says. “Religion and politics, from Reagan on, has really changed politics for the worse in my opinion. This was the birth of that.”

Continue reading...
items.t: ‘Shakespearean tale of ego, greed and ambition’: the scandalous story of televangelism

items.title: Early Christian fresco of Jesus found near ancient Nicaea
items.summary:
Archaeologists working near the Turkish town of Iznik have uncovered a rare fresco of Jesus Christ inside a 3rd-century underground tomb: a painting so well-preserved that it is now considered one of the most significant finds in early Christian archaeology in the region. The image, found during excavations at Hisardere Necropolis in August 2025, depicts Jesus as the Good Shepherd: a young, clean-shaven man in a Roman tunic, carrying a goat across his shoulders, surrounded by other animals and flowering vegetation. Lead archaeologist Gülsen Kutbay has described it as possibly the only known example of its kind in Anatolia, the vast historical territory that covers most of modern-day Türkiye. The Good Shepherd was one of the central images of early Christianity. In the decades and centuries before the cross became the universal emblem of Christian faith, it expressed protection, salvation, and divine guidance, drawn directly from the Gospel of John. “I am the good shepherd,” Read More…

items.title: Ukrainian bishop: Finding joy and hope amid war
items.summary:
Bishop Radosław Zmitrowicz, auxiliary bishop of the Diocese of Kamianets-Podilskyi in Ukraine, recently visited the Franciscan church in Jasło, Poland. He preached homilies throughout the day and, after the Masses, stood holding a collection basket to raise money for a Catholic school in Ukraine. In an interview with Aleteia, he discusses the realities of life in a country at war, the witness of faith and hope, and an innovative approach to Catholic education. Aleteia: We receive all kinds of reports from Ukraine, but hearing someone who lives and ministers there every day speak about this reality with genuine joy and hope despite everything is deeply moving. How is it possible for people living in the midst of the nightmare of war to preserve peace in their hearts? Bishop Radosław Zmitrowicz: I’ll begin with an image that might not seem particularly pious at first. When the war broke out, we all experienced tremendous fear and panic. Read More…

items.title: How a painting of Mary became Our Lady of La Salette
items.summary:
French painter Louise Groux has been sharing her vibrant, colorful artwork on social media since 2021. In late October, she found that the face of Our Lady of La Salette was emerging from one of her paintings. For Groux, the work speaks to the turmoil that has shaken France in recent years. “Painting also means being willing to search, to doubt, to let yourself be taken in a new direction … and sometimes to discover something on the canvas that you hadn’t planned.” That’s how Groux described her experience in an Instagram video posted on October 21, 2026, which has been viewed nearly 28,000 times. In the video, she tells the story of a painting of the Virgin Mary, initially dressed in the colors of the French flag. To the artist’s surprise, as she worked, the image gradually began to take on the appearance of Our Lady of La Salette. Although Groux knew little about Read More…

items.title: Is the Presentation of Mary found in the Bible?
items.summary:
Generally speaking, the Catholic Church celebrates both biblical events and canonized saints throughout the liturgical year, paying special attention to the events central to salvation history. On occasion, there will be certain events that aren’t explicitly mentioned in Scripture, but that come from central beliefs, such as Mary’s Immaculate Conception. There are also a select few feasts that are solely based in “tradition,” having been celebrated early on and remaining on the calendar 2,000 years later. The feast of the Presentation of the Blessed Virgin Mary is one of those feasts, not having any basis in a biblical event but in a tradition that was preserved by the early Church. The Presentation of the Mary is based on an ancient text from the year 145 called The Protoevangelium of James, a text that was highly revered by early Christians and widely circulated at the time. In it, we find the Virgin Mary’s parents entrusting her to the Jewish Read More… 

Is the Presentation of Mary found in the Bible?
items.t: Is the Presentation of Mary found in the Bible?

items.title: Catholic co-founder of Pizza Hut dies at 95
items.summary:
Catholic co-founder of Pizza Hut, Dan Carney, age 95, died this week in Kansas. His life is an example of living with a vision, willingness to work hard, and trust in God’s plan to see a mission accomplished. He is also an example of what you do once you’ve reached success by giving back to his community and to his Church. Born in 1931, Dan grew up in Kansas in a devout Catholic home as the oldest of 12 siblings. He learned the importance of his faith at a young age, walking daily to Blessed Sacrament Church in Wichita to serve as an altar boy at 6:30 a.m. Mass. His family and obituaries describe him as guided by his Catholic faith and as a “humble servant of God.” Developing strong habits of faith at a young age helped him throughout his life. In 1948, while Dan was just 17 years old, his father, Michael, died. Read More…

items.title: Why AI can never satisfy our need for real human relationships
items.summary:
In recent years, artificial intelligence has become much more than a search engine and is increasingly being used by individuals around the world as a replacement for human relationships. AI chatbots can appear very friendly and kind, giving positive encouragement and offering funny jokes to lighten our mood. Not only that, chatbots are always there, ready and waiting to interact with us. They never cancel appointments or say bad things about us, and always say exactly what we want them to say. It’s no surprise that many of us “talk” with our chatbots for hours on end, pouring our heart out into the chat, communicating with something that always listens and never interrupts. Yet, while it may seem like an ideal situation, the reality is that these machines cannot satisfy our deepest human longings for relationship. items.title: The day St. Peter’s dome was crowned with a cross
items.summary:
On November 18, 1593, a feverish excitement grips the streets of Rome. We can imagine Pope Clement VIII making his way to the Sistine Chapel to pray beneath the ceiling Michelangelo covered with frescoes more than 80 years earlier. What he prays for remains a mystery, but it’s a safe bet that his mind is not on the routine business of the Curia. On this cold but bright morning, all his subjects have their eyes fixed on the sky, where the enormous, majestic dome of St. Peter’s rises above the city. Designed by Michelangelo, drawing on Bramante’s original vision, and completed by Giacomo della Porta, this architectural marvel awaits its final adornment. The Cupolone, as Romans are beginning to call it, is already crowned by a lantern rising nearly 430 feet above the city. At that dizzying height, workers scurry like ants across wooden scaffolding suspended in midair, under della Porta’s direction. The enormous gilded Read More…

items.title: The serious reason behind Thank Your Priest campaign
items.summary:
We smile and say hello to them every Sunday at Mass, and tell them our deepest, darkest secrets in the confessional. They baptize our children, witness our marriages, and give us the Anointing when we fall ill. We depend on our priests, and we appreciate all they do. But do we ever stop to think about how they’re doing?  Are they tired? Burned out, even? The burden of caring for so many people’s spiritual welfare can be a lot. And, they have to face all the practical worries we face too: Have we made enough to cover the light bill this month? Who should we hire to pave the sidewalk? With all that they carry on their shoulders every day, we might wonder, frankly, how is their mental health? Maybe we should be thinking more about our priests’ mental health. items.title: Pink Rabbit: the provocative bedroom drama about a Muslim OnlyFans star interrupted by her mum
items.summary:
In Farah Ashraf’s solo show an obedient daughter secretly does online sex work as ‘PersianBaby’. The actor and writer explains how two worlds collide in her darkly funny play

At home, Amna is the modest and dutiful Muslim daughter of her parents’ dreams. Online, armed with a webcam and an OnlyFans account, she is PersianBaby – an exoticised version of herself complete with fake accent, designed to entice men willing to part with their cash.

Pink Rabbit, writer-performer Farah Ashraf’s provocative and darkly funny solo play, is a nuanced account of being caught between the private life of desire and the cultural expectations that shape how she is perceived. “I loved this idea of push and pull, and two different worlds,” says Ashraf who began work on the play during her final year at the Oxford School of Drama, before which she had trained with the National Youth Theatre.

items.title: US Catholic bishops’ new AI task force urges regulation and worker protections
items.summary:
U.S. Catholic bishops are calling for guardrails on artificial intelligence as the Catholic Church seeks to protect humanity while technology advances.

They are following Pope Leo’s lead, who has said that AI is humanity’s biggest challenge today. His first encyclical, “Magnifica Humanitas”, called for robust AI regulation.

Bishop Oscar Cantú of San Jose, California, emphasized the unique role the U.S. church is well-positioned to play when he addressed his colleagues at the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops’ annual fall gathering Wednesday. From his Silicon Valley diocese, Cantú chairs the conference’s new AI task force focused on preserving human dignity.

“The Church possesses something that Silicon Valley cannot engineer: over 2,000 years of wisdom on the human person, on truth, and on the common good,” Cantú said.

The bishops have been meeting with tech company executives and political leaders to discuss AI, much of which is developed in the U.S. Cantú told the gathering in Baltimore that the task force will help lobby lawmakers for “clear guardrails on the development and use of AI.” The group “will continue monitoring labor impacts and advocating for workers.”

Bishops are particularly concerned about young people’s use of AI. The task force hopes to become a clearinghouse on best practices and AI literacy.

“The Church’s contribution is to insist that every human being possesses inherent dignity that no algorithm can measure and no market can price,” Cantú said.

The bishops also approved updates to their investing guidelines, which are used by other Catholic…
items.t: US Catholic bishops’ new AI task force urges regulation and worker protections

items.title: St. Peter’s Basilica marks 400 years at the heart of the Catholic Church
items.summary:
ROME — St. Peter’s Basilica, the spiritual heart of Catholicism whose commanding dome defines the Roman skyline and is a monument to artistic achievement and perseverance, marked the 400th anniversary of its dedication on Wednesday.

Pope Leo XIV dedicated a Mass “to one of the most celebrated monuments in the world,” telling the faithful gathered beneath the basilica’s soaring vaults that “visiting this majestic church always stirs emotion: We are filled with awe, inspired by the sacredness of faith, the power of history and the beauty of art.”

The Chicago-born pontiff also reflected on the scale of the structure, which stretches roughly the length of two American football fields.

“The vastness of the Vatican Basilica reflects an enduring vocation to welcome, so that as many people as possible may find a place in the church,” Leo said.

St. Peter’s construction spanned 120 years, 20 pontificates and the work of a succession of 12 architects, enduring the Protestant Reformation, which started in 1517, and the Sack of Rome in 1527 before Pope Urban VIII dedicated it on Nov. 18, 1626.

“You walk through those doors and you won’t feel the conflicts and the disasters and the setbacks,” said Elizabeth Lev, a Rome-based American art historian. “You walk through those doors and you see continuity and beauty and achievement and triumph.”

A setting for papal ceremonies and a destination for millions of pilgrims each year, the basilica was built over the traditional burial site of the Apostle Peter, replacing a church that had stood for more than a millennium.

Pope Julius II…
items.t: St. Peter’s Basilica marks 400 years at the heart of the Catholic Church

items.title: Mexico’s Catholic street DJs turn annual Marian pilgrimage into a party
items.summary:
MEXICO CITY — A sea of people carrying statues of Mexico’s patron saint, the Virgin of Guadalupe, marched along the avenue leading up to the country’s most important basilica on Wednesday.

Such pilgrimages are practically embedded in the daily rhythms of the bustling Mexican capital. But the roughly 1,000 pilgrims from across the Latin American nation aren’t just Catholic devotees.

They’re also Mexican street DJs.

The annual procession and street party known as the “sonidero” pilgrimage is perhaps one of the most Mexico City-esque convergences of celebrations to hit the city.

Sonideros, as they’re known, are a particular brand of DJs found primarily in Mexico City, but also in other parts of Mexico and Colombia. The DJs mix rhythmic tunes of cumbia with radio announcements, chanting shout outs that mingle with the music.

The tradition is so important in the city, particularly in working-class neighborhoods, that in 2023 the city government recognized sonidero culture as intangible cultural heritage — a designation UNESCO quickly celebrated. The music has even evolved into its own dance, a derivation of cumbia that has more open steps meant for street parties than the classic two-person cumbia.

Each neighborhood has its own set of sonideros who organize pop-up mobile parties. Wednesday’s party-procession on the avenue leading up to the famed Basilica de Guadalupe wasn’t so spontaneous, but rather part of an annual celebration now spanning decades.

“The root of faith in Mexico is the Virgin of Guadalupe,” said Christian Castañeda, a musician who joined the throngs of…
items.t: Mexico’s Catholic street DJs turn annual pilgrimage into a party

items.title: Pope prays with Irish archbishop and families of the disappeared during ‘The Troubles’
items.summary:
Pope Leo XIV met on Wednesday with Ireland’s senior archbishop and the families of people who went missing during The Troubles. 

A period of violent conflict over the question whether Northern Ireland should remain part of the United Kingdom or join a united Ireland, The Troubles unfolded between the late 1960s and the signing of the Good Friday Agreement in 1998.

Archbishop Eamon Martin of Armagh, Primate of All Ireland, joined the pope and family members of 17 people believed to have been abducted, killed and secretly buried during The Troubles by Irish republican paramilitary groups.

After the weekly General Audience on Wednesday, Leo recited a special prayer with the archbishop and family members, asking for the return of the Disappeared.

The bodies of 13 of the 17 have been found, but the remains of four are still missing. 

A fifth person, Lisa Dorrian, disappeared in 2005 and is also considered one of the Disappeared by some campaigners.

Dorrian’s case, however, falls outside the remit of the Independent Commission for the Location of Victims’ Remains, a joint body of the Irish and British governments established in 1999 to find the burial sites of the Disappeared.

“From the bottom of [my] heart I implore anyone with information to please come forward and show mercy so that the remaining families can give their loved ones the dignity of a Christian burial,” Martin said after the meeting.

Violence mainly took place in Northern Ireland, but it spilled over into the Republic of Ireland, England, and even parts of Europe.

“I wish to thank God for those who have…
items.t: Pope prays with Irish archbishop and families of the disappeared during ‘The Troubles’

items.title: Pope Leo celebrates 400 years of St. Peter’s

As we mark 400 years since the dedication of the current Basilica of St. Peter’s, Pope Leo offers insight into why this feast is so important. Here’s his homily from evening Mass on November 18. ~ Dear brothers and sisters, The feast that gathers us together today in joy poses a question to each of us: what did we feel when we entered Saint Peter’s Basilica?  A visit to this majestic church always moves us.  We are filled with awe, stirred by the sacredness of faith, the power of history and the beauty of art.  And yet all of this rests upon a humble tomb: that of the fisherman of Galilee, Simon son of Jonah.  Why has this burial place become one of the most celebrated monuments in the whole world, at the heart of Catholicism?  The Gospel we have heard (Mt 16:13-19) gives us the answer, recounting the faith of a man who, at the will Read More…

items.title: A surprising way to fight isolation and loneliness
items.summary:
I spent seven years as a Carmelite brother, during which time I lived in monasteries. One Sunday during this time, a relative of mine came to visit with her children. As evening fell, we walked together on the monastery grounds perched in the hidden hills of northern California before she headed home. The parking lot was empty, and a deep quiet had settled in. From the outside, the place could have seemed abandoned. “Don’t you get lonely here?” she asked. Her question surprised me. Of course, monks experience loneliness, too. But it wasn’t the defining experience of my life there. Prayer nourished my sense of God’s presence, and the brothers around me had become a family. That evening has stayed with me because so many people experience the reverse: full calendars, constant messages, plenty of people nearby … and simultaneously a sense of disconnection – or even loneliness. items.title: Rethinking the collection basket with eCatholic
items.summary:
Every week, perhaps we don’t think much of it when the collection basket comes around at church. But what would happen if we saw our offertory at Mass as something with great spiritual value? Sharing the deep significance behind this sometimes-mundane act of giving is at the heart of an insightful new book from eCatholic, a tech platform for Catholic dioceses. The new book is called The Generous Parish, and it’s a practical guide written to help pastors and parish leaders recover the Church’s theology of giving. (You can read the free digital version here.) Many Catholics have never really thought about the theological reasons for giving. items.title: Kraków basilica holds Mass for man who committed deadly terror attack
items.summary:
On Monday, an iconic Kraków basilica held a Mass for the soul of the man who killed six in the city earlier this month.

Michał Oksiński shot six dead and injured at least 15 earlier this month just meters away from where the church is. He also killed his parents and sister before the Nov. 7 attack.

Following surprise on social media at the church’s decision, St Mary’s Basilica said the Mass “in no way indicates justification for the crime” and is “an expression of the Christian faith in God’s mercy.”

On Sunday, a former city councillor, Łukasz Wantuch, shared online a picture of the announcement that the Mass would be held Monday morning at the basilica for “the late Michał Oksiński and the deceased members of his family.”

“I won’t hide the fact that I find this somewhat shocking,” he said.

“But perhaps that is what faith is about: praying even for a murderer,” he added in a Facebook post that garnered over 1000 comments.

Later that day, the basilica shared a statement from parish administrator Father Mariusz Słonina, which said the mass “is a private initiative of one of the priests, not of St Mary’s Parish.”

However, the statement added  “praying for the deceased is an expression of the Christian faith in God’s mercy” and “in no way indicates justification for the crime, a lessening of the perpetrator’s responsibility, or a trivialization of the suffering of the victims.”

According to local news service KR24, there were roughly a dozen people in attendance at the mass, with three priests presiding over the mass. 

There were uniformed police officers outside the…
items.t: Kraków basilica holds mass for man who committed deadly terror attack

items.title: Pope Leo’s envoy brings message of comfort and unity to Holy Land Christians
items.summary:
JERUSALEM — The Vatican cardinal who oversees care of the Catholic faithful in the Holy Land visited Jerusalem on Tuesday, saying he wanted to convey the presence of Pope Leo XIV during particularly troubled times for Christians in the region.

Cardinal Claudio Gugerotti, prefect of the Vatican’s Dicastery for the Eastern Churches, prayed before the Holy Edicule inside the Church of the Holy Sepulcher, which marks the site where Christians believe Jesus was buried and rose from the dead.

“Lord, you were here physically,” Gugerotti prayed. “Lord, give hope to the world.”

Leaders of other Christian denominations in Jerusalem listened intently. The incense-filled ceremony, with clergy in solemn robes, offered a show of unity in the basilica where they have sometimes tensely shared worship space in a unique arrangement dating to the 19th century.

Preceded by bagpipers, rows of Franciscan friars and a large cross, Gugerotti and other Christian leaders processed through the narrow stone alleyways of Jerusalem’s Old City to the centuries-old church.

Harassment of clergy and faithful there has been rising. A rare violent attack on a religious sister in April sent shock waves across Israel.

“We know we are not always welcome,” said Sister Marie Reine, a Catholic nun who joined the procession in her white habit. “But our presence can bring peace, too.”

Most of Israel’s Christians are Palestinians, who have been the target of heated rhetoric after Arab-led parties made historic gains in the national elections last month. And neighboring Jordan is reeling from an attack that…
items.t: Pope Leo’s envoy brings message of comfort and unity to Holy Land Christians

items.title: James Talarico’s ‘love thy neighbour’ message won over Texas. Is Australia ready to embrace a new Christian left? | Brigid Delaney
items.summary:
The Democrat tapped into a hunger for politics with more moral authority. But in Australia, overt displays of Christianity have been met with discomfort – even cynicism

There was a time, within living memory, when Australian Christianity had a definable and active left wing: Palm Sunday peace marches, guitar masses, priests coming home from far-flung missions with stories of liberation theology and, in the early 2000s, powerful and sustained activism against government policies of mandatory detention.

For the left wing of the church, Jesus was an anti-capitalist who smashed the tables of the money lenders and told a wealthy young man to sell his possessions, give to the poor and follow him – for it was easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than a rich man to enter heaven.
